correctness.rationale: Exhaustive independent enumeration of all legal subsets of at most six of twenty-four arcs matches a backtracker: 3301 augmented faces. The checker constructs 1608 augmented pairs, exhaustively verifies 13104 Hasse incidences have no directed matching cycle, and reduces the 37-by-48 signed integer Morse boundary to the zero matrix. The resulting one-vertex, 37-three-cell, 48-four-cell CW model has null 4-cell attaching maps by the degree/Hurewicz isomorphism. Independently computed mod-two boundary ranks corroborate both Betti ranks. Every finite premise has a standalone executable certificate.

evidence: The 2022 Euler formula specializes to a 12-arc one-way orientation; it is not the signed chain complex of the 24-arc bidirected object. The published 2026 homology formulas are for bidirectional polygons, not bidirected complete bipartite graphs. claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: One-direction complete bipartite multipaths are ordinary chessboard matchings (only twelve arc vertices), not the twenty-four-arc bidirected, cycle-containing object. Bidirectional path/polygon results exclude complete bipartite graphs; the acyclic blow-up comparison cannot apply because directed two-cycles exist. Previously indexed bidirected K_{3,3} and K_{2,n} computations involve different graph parameters, and do not imply the result for K_{3,4}. Two-matching and ordinary Morse complexes of undirected K_{3,4} have different simplex objects. The present exact ranks and homotopy type are not obtained from Euler characteristic alone.

value.rationale: The smallest unbalanced complete bipartite bidirected graph with both partition sizes at least three is a canonical first nontrivial two-sided branching test case. Its integral homotopy type is not implied by known Euler counts; the two distinct homology dimensions and nonzero lower-dimensional classes in a pure five-dimensional complex give a structural nonshellability boundary. The result excludes torsion for this explicitly natural test graph by exact integral Morse reduction. It is a finite exact classification; no family theorem is implied.
